**In Praise of Moss**

Moss is easy to overlook. It doesn't flower or tower, and it never demands attention. It just shows up on north-facing stones, in sidewalk cracks, on the shingles of houses whose owners have stopped fighting it. And yet moss is one of the great success stories of life on Earth.

Mosses were among the first plants to leave the water, roughly 450 million years ago. They did it without roots, without seeds, without the vascular plumbing that lets trees drink from deep underground. They simply learned to wait. Many mosses can dry out almost completely, turning brittle and brown, and remain that way for years. Then a single rain arrives, and within hours they unfurl green again, as if nothing happened. Some specimens revived after centuries frozen beneath Antarctic ice.

There's something instructive in that. We tend to admire resilience that looks like force: the oak splitting rock, the salmon leaping upstream. Moss offers a different model. Its strength is patience, a willingness to go dormant rather than break, to accept that conditions are sometimes wrong and to be ready when they turn right.

Moss also builds the world for others. It holds soil in place, soaks up water like a sponge, and shelters tiny creatures such as tardigrades and springtails, whole ecosystems in a patch smaller than your palm.

Next time you pass a mossy wall, it's worth pausing. You're looking at a lineage older than dinosaurs, quietly succeeding by being small, slow, and persistent.
